Star Ratings Pod 1, Condition 1: Where Do Rating Differences Feel Bigger?

Author

Jamie C. Lee

Published

October 15, 2026

Part 1: What this report does

The question

Each participant saw pairs of star ratings and said how different the two ratings felt, on a 0–100 slider. Every pair is the same distance apart (0.4 stars): 1.0 vs 1.4, 1.1 vs 1.5, and so on up to 4.6 vs 5.0. If people read the scale literally, every pair would feel equally different and the curve of responses would be flat.

Where the curve rises, a 0.4-star gap feels bigger than it is. A sudden rise suggests a boundary: a point where ratings switch category (for example from “okay” to “good”), so pairs that cross it feel extra different. The question is where these boundaries are, and whether the scale splits into regions such as negative, neutral and positive.

Data. 167 condition 1 participants (1-to-5 scale only) who passed the attention checks. Each rated all 37 pairs. Each pair is placed at its midpoint (1.0 vs 1.4 sits at 1.2), so the curve runs from 1.2 to 4.8.

The tests, and why each one is run

# Test Question it answers Why it’s needed
1 Average curve What does the typical response look like across the scale? The starting point: shows where differences feel bigger.
2 Where the curve rises Is the rise smooth, or does it come in spurts? Spurts point to boundaries; a smooth rise does not.
3 How many regions? Is the scale best described as 1, 2, 3 or 4 regions? Tells us how many boundaries the data support.
4 Where the boundaries are Where do the breaks between regions fall, and how stable is that? A boundary that moves around with the sample is not trustworthy.
5 Slopes within regions Inside each region, do differences still grow, or stay flat? A flat region means the scale is perceived evenly there.
6 A model of how good each rating feels (β-δ) Can one model explain the whole curve: a smooth change in sensitivity (δ) plus jumps in value at whole stars (β)? Tests 3–5 describe the curve; this explains why it looks that way, and tests specific ideas: Weber’s law, left-digit effects, a special 4-star boundary.
7 Robustness Do the results hold without the top pair, with all participants, and for people who use the slider narrowly vs widely? Checks the conclusions don’t hinge on one pair, on the exclusion rule, or on a few wide-range responders.

How the region models work

A region model splits the scale at one or more breaks and fits a straight line in each region. The breaks are found by trying every possible location and keeping the one whose lines sit closest to the average curve. Each region must contain at least 5 of the 37 pairs.

Two kinds of region model are fitted:

  • Step: each region gets its own line, so the curve can jump at a break. A sharp category boundary would look like this.
  • Elbow: the lines must connect, so the curve can only bend at a break. A gradual shift would look like this.

The step models fit these data much better (Appendix A), so the main results use them.

Terms used in the results

  • Prediction test. The fairest way to compare 2, 3 or 4 regions. Participants are randomly split in half. Half A is used to place the breaks and lines; the result is then checked against half B’s average curve, which played no part in fitting. A model with too many regions bends to fit noise in half A and predicts half B worse. Repeated over 200 random splits. Lower prediction error = better.
  • BIC. A fit score that penalizes extra regions. Lower = better; differences under about 6 are close to ties. It uses the same data to place the breaks and to score them, which flatters models with more regions, so it is the secondary measure here.
  • Bootstrap. Participants are re-drawn at random (with repeats) 2000 times, and the whole analysis is re-run each time. How much the breaks and slopes move across re-draws shows how certain they are. Slope p-values and 95% intervals come from here.
  • Slope. How much the perceived difference changes per star within a region, in slider points. A slope of 0 means a 0.4-star gap feels equally large throughout the region.

Part 2: Key results

  • The average curve rises from 19 points at the bottom of the scale to 65 at the top, and it rises in spurts rather than smoothly (tests 1–2).
  • The best explanation is a smooth rise in sensitivity plus jumps at whole stars (test 6). This model predicts new participants better than any region model (prediction error 5.3 vs 7.0; lower = better) and comes close to the raw averages (5.0).
    1. Sensitivity grows toward the top. A 0.4-star difference near 5 stars feels about 2.1 times as large as the same difference near 1 star. Weber’s law, which predicts the opposite, fits very poorly.
    2. Value jumps at every whole star. The jumps are equal at 2 and 3 stars (about 3.7 points each) and about twice as large at 4 stars (7.0; p < .0005 vs 2 stars). The jump at 5 stars (8.2) is not clearly larger than at 4.
    3. A left-digit effect explains most of the jumps (people discount about 4% of the decimal part), but not all of them. 3 stars is a weaker boundary (p = .009) and 4 stars a stronger one (p = .060, borderline) than a pure left-digit effect predicts.
    4. There is no lasting shift in sensitivity near 4 stars. Once the smooth rise and the 4-star jump are in the model, adding one does not help.
    5. Slider use (test 7). The rising sensitivity and the whole-star jumps hold for both wide- and narrow-range slider users. The extra-large 4-star jump is clear among wide-range users (2.1 times the 2- and 3-star jumps) but uncertain among narrow-range users (1.5 times, interval includes 1). When each person’s answers are put on their own scale, so everyone counts equally, the 4-star jump is still 1.6 times the others (p = .004). It is the least robust finding, but it holds up.
  • Seen as regions (tests 3–5), the same curve splits into three: a steady rise up to 3.75 stars, a jump of about 11 points into a flat stretch around 4 stars, then a steep climb toward 5. Three regions beat two (prediction error 7.0 vs 10.9), even without the top pair. Test 6 explains these regions: the jump is the 4-star jump, the flat stretch is the curve settling back after it, and the climb is rising sensitivity plus the jump at 5.
  • Bottom line: the scale is not split into negative / neutral / positive around its midpoint. Differences feel larger the higher the ratings, each whole star works as a small category boundary, and 4 stars is the strongest boundary inside the scale, consistent with “4 stars = good”. These labels are an interpretation of the fitted shapes, not something the models test directly.

Part 3: Results

Test 1: The average curve

The thick line is the average response at each pair, with its 95% confidence band; thin gray lines are individual participants. Magenta diamonds mark pairs that straddle a whole star (for example 2.8 vs 3.2), in this and every later plot.

Show code 
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = long, aes(x, y, group = id), color = "#9a9893", alpha = 0.10, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(data = mean_curve, aes(x, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = blue, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(data = mean_curve, aes(x, m), color = blue, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_line(data = filter(mean_curve, cross), aes(x, m, group = block), color = magenta, linewidth = 1.6) +
  cross_points(mean_curve, 2.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 5, 0.5)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Midpoint of the rating pair (stars)", y = "Perceived difference (0-100)",
       title = "Average perceived difference across the 1-to-5 scale") +
  theme_pod

Test 2: Where the curve rises

A smooth curve is fitted through all responses (a GAM, allowing each person their own baseline and tilt). The lower panel shows how steep it is at each point. Shaded spans are where the curve is clearly rising (the 95% interval of its steepness is above 0).

Show code 
shade <- geom_rect(data = rise_spans, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
                   fill = orange, alpha = 0.12)
p1 <- ggplot() + shade +
  geom_ribbon(data = gam_curve, aes(x, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = blue, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(data = gam_curve, aes(x, fit), color = blue, linewidth = 1.1) +
  cross_points(mean_curve, 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 5, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Perceived difference", title = "Smoothed average curve (points = raw averages)") +
  theme_pod
p2 <- ggplot() + shade +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = ink2, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_ribbon(data = gam_deriv, aes(x, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = blue, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(data = gam_deriv, aes(x, d), color = blue, linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 5, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Midpoint of the rating pair (stars)", y = "Steepness (points per star)",
       title = "How steep the curve is; shaded = clearly rising") +
  theme_pod
p1 / p2

Result. The curve rises in 4 separate spurts (1.5-1.8, 2.4-2.9, 3.4-3.9, 4.4-4.8 stars) with flat stretches between them. Each spurt ends where pairs begin to straddle a whole star. That staircase shape is what tests 3–6 try to explain.

Test 3: How many regions?

Each row is one model. Prediction error is the main measure (lower = better): how far the curve fitted on one half of participants misses the other half. Best in % of splits is how often that model had the lowest error among the region models. The last row is a benchmark that reuses half A’s raw averages with no model at all.

Result.

  • 3 regions beat 2. The 3-region step model predicts new participants clearly better than the 2-region one, with all pairs (7.0 vs 10.9) and without the top pair (7.0 vs 8.0). BIC agrees.
  • 4 regions barely help. The 4-region model is best in more splits, but by a hair (6.9 vs 7.0). Its extra break (2.15) just follows the bump where pairs cross 2 stars, and BIC prefers 3 regions. Three is the best balance.
  • Jumps beat bends. Every step model predicts better than the elbow model with the same number of regions.
  • The 3-region step model beats whole-star bumps on a straight-line trend (7.0 vs 8.1). But Test 6 shows that whole-star jumps on a curved trend beat every region model.
  • No region model matches the raw averages (5.0). Some pair-to-pair detail repeats across halves of the sample but is finer than straight-line regions can capture. Test 6 gets much closer.

Test 4: Where the boundaries are, and how stable they are

For each break, the table shows its best estimate and how often it lands in the same spot when participants are re-drawn. At the allowed limit is how often a break sits at the edge of where the method can put it (each region needs 5 pairs). A break that piles up there is trying to isolate the scale’s end, not marking a boundary.

All 37 pairs

Show code 
show_breaks(R_all, c("step1", "step2"))

Step, 2 regions (1 break) Only break 3.65 3.65-4.35 67% 76% 22%
Step, 3 regions (2 breaks) Lower break 3.75 3.65-3.75 81% 99% 0%
Step, 3 regions (2 breaks) Upper break 4.35 4.25-4.35 92% 98% 92%

Result. The 3-region model’s first boundary is stable: with all pairs it lands at 3.75 in 81% of re-draws and within 0.1 stars in 99%. Without the top pair it is less sharply pinned (within 0.1 stars in 90%). The second boundary sits at the allowed limit in most re-draws (92% with all pairs, 67% without the top pair), so it marks where the climb toward 5 stars begins. The 2-region model’s single break (3.65) wanders much more with all pairs (95% range 3.65-4.35): with only one break, it is pulled between the jump near 4 stars and the climb at the top.

Result. In the 3-region model, the slope is clearly positive below the first boundary and in the top region, and not different from 0 in the middle region (with all pairs and without the top pair). In the 2-region model both slopes are positive, but its second region lumps the flat stretch around 4 stars together with the climb to 5, so its slope averages over two different patterns.

Two further checks of the same slopes are in Appendix B: a mixed model on all individual responses, and a split-half test. They agree that the first and last regions rise, and none finds the 3-region model’s middle slope different from 0. The closest is the mixed model with all pairs (slightly negative, p = .055). One exception: in the 2-region model with all pairs, half A placed its break at the top of the scale instead of near 4 stars, so that row tests different regions.

Test 6: A model of how good each rating feels (β-δ)

The idea

Tests 3–5 fit straight lines to the differences people report. That describes the curve but does not say why it looks the way it does. This test goes one level deeper and models how good each rating feels, then derives the differences from that.

The model borrows its structure from quasi-hyperbolic (β-δ) discounting and from left-digit models of prices (Thomas & Morwitz, 2005) and odometer readings (Lacetera, Pope & Sydnor, 2012). Each combines two ingredients:

  • δ, a smooth part: how sensitive people are to a change in rating at each point on the scale.
  • β, jumps: a one-off step up in how good a rating feels when it reaches a privileged point. Here the candidates are the whole stars 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Why this matters for reading the curve. The task measures differences between two ratings 0.4 stars apart. A jump in value at, say, 4 stars only affects pairs that straddle 4 (3.6 vs 4.0 through 3.9 vs 4.3). Those four pairs feel bigger, and the curve then drops back. That is exactly the magenta blocks in the plots. A change in sensitivity would instead make differences stay bigger from that point on. The two ingredients therefore leave different fingerprints, and the model can tell them apart.

The model

\[\text{response}(a) = \text{offset} + u(a + 0.4) - u(a)\]

\[u(r) = \lambda \cdot \big[-\log(T - r)\big] + \beta_2\,\mathbf{1}[r \ge 2] + \beta_3\,\mathbf{1}[r \ge 3] + \beta_4\,\mathbf{1}[r \ge 4] + \beta_5\,\mathbf{1}[r \ge 5]\]

  • \(a\) = the lower rating in a pair (1.0 to 4.6 stars); the higher rating is \(a + 0.4\).
  • \(\text{response}(a)\) = the average perceived difference for that pair, on the 0–100 slider.
  • \(r\) = any star rating from 1 to 5.
  • \(u(r)\) = how good rating \(r\) feels (its perceived value), in slider points. Only differences in \(u\) matter, so its zero point is arbitrary.
  • \(\text{offset}\) = a constant that absorbs how people use the slider overall. It shifts every response equally and does not affect the shape.
  • \(\lambda\) (lambda) = the strength of the smooth part: how many slider points a change in rating is worth, overall.
  • \(T\) = the anchor of the “distance from perfect” curve, in stars (above 5). The term \(-\log(T - r)\) rises faster as \(r\) approaches \(T\), so sensitivity grows toward the top of the scale. A larger \(T\) means gentler curvature; as \(T\) grows very large the curve becomes a straight line.
  • \(\log\) = natural logarithm.
  • \(\beta_2, \beta_3, \beta_4, \beta_5\) (beta) = the size of the jump in value, in slider points, when a rating reaches 2, 3, 4 or 5 stars.
  • \(\mathbf{1}[r \ge k]\) = 1 if rating \(r\) is at least \(k\) stars, otherwise 0. It switches the jump on.

The left-digit version replaces every rating \(r\) with \(\hat r = \lfloor r \rfloor + (1 - \theta)(r - \lfloor r \rfloor)\) inside the smooth part and drops the separate jumps:

  • \(\lfloor r \rfloor\) = the whole-star part of \(r\) (for 3.7, it is 3).
  • \(\theta\) (theta) = the share of the decimal part that people ignore, between 0 and 1. With \(\theta = 0.1\), a 3.7 is read as \(3 + 0.9 \times 0.7 = 3.63\).
  • \(\hat r\) = the rating as perceived. Ignoring part of the decimal creates a jump at every whole star automatically. Its size is set by \(\theta\) and by how sensitive people are at that point, so one number explains all the jumps.

How it is fitted. As with the region models, the few shape settings (\(T\), and \(\theta\) for the left-digit version) are found by trying a grid of values and keeping the best fit. Everything else is then estimated directly. Models are compared with the same prediction test (the same 200 half-splits as Test 3), and uncertainty comes from the same participant bootstrap.

The model is built up in four steps. Each adds one ingredient and keeps it only if it improves prediction.

Step 1: The smooth part. Which way does sensitivity change?

Question. Ignoring jumps, how does sensitivity change along the scale?

Why. Different theories predict different shapes. Weber’s law, the classic account of perception, says people are most sensitive at the bottom of a scale, so differences should shrink as ratings rise. A “distance from perfect” reading says people judge a rating by how far it falls short of 5, so differences should grow near the top. A straight line is the neutral benchmark.

Show code 
show_lev <- function(keys) lev_cmp |>
  filter(key %in% keys) |>
  arrange(match(key, keys)) |>
  transmute(Model = lev_labels[key], `Prediction error` = sprintf("%.1f", err),
            `Δ BIC` = ifelse(is.na(dBIC), "-", sprintf("%.1f", dBIC))) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")
show_lev(c("flat", "linear", "weber", "perfect"))
Model Prediction error Δ BIC
Flat: same sensitivity everywhere 141.8 3095.1
Straight-line rise 14.9 269.7
Weber-Fechner: most sensitive at the bottom 42.4 1000.9
Distance from perfect: most sensitive near 5 11.3 171.1

Result. “Distance from perfect” predicts best (11.3, against 14.9 for a straight line). Weber’s law fits far worse than a straight line (42.4): it predicts the wrong direction. Sensitivity grows toward the top of the scale. This smooth curve is used in all later steps.

Step 2: Jumps at whole stars

Question. On top of the smooth part, does value jump when a rating reaches a whole star? Are the jumps the same size at every whole star?

Why. The magenta blocks in Test 1 suggest jumps. If all jumps are equal, a simple left-digit effect is enough. If one is larger, that whole star is a special boundary. Four versions are compared: separate jumps; one shared jump at 2, 3 and 4; equal jumps at 2 and 3 with separate jumps at 4 and 5; and the left-digit version, where one setting (\(\theta\)) produces every jump.

Show code 
show_lev(c("perfect", "beta", "shared", "b23", "leftdig"))
Model Prediction error Δ BIC
Distance from perfect: most sensitive near 5 11.3 171.1
+ separate jump at 2, 3, 4 and 5 5.3 16.2
+ one shared jump at 2, 3, 4 (own jump at 5) 5.8 17.7
+ equal jumps at 2 and 3, own jumps at 4 and 5 5.3 7.5
+ left-digit: one inattention setting makes every jump 5.4 0.0

Jump sizes (separate-jumps model; slider points; 95% intervals from the bootstrap):

Does one left-digit setting explain every jump? Each row compares a freely estimated jump with what the left-digit model implies for the same re-drawn sample:

Show code 
ld_vs_free |>
  transmute(`Whole star` = k, `Free jump` = sprintf("%.1f", free),
            `Left-digit implies` = sprintf("%.1f", implied),
            `Free minus implied` = sprintf("%.1f", free - implied),
            `95% CI` = sapply(draws, ci), p = sapply(draws, pboot)) |>
  kable(align = "rrrrrr")
Whole star Free jump Left-digit implies Free minus implied 95% CI p
2 3.8 3.9 -0.2 -1.2 to 0.7 .636
3 3.7 4.7 -1.1 -2.0 to -0.3 .009
4 7.0 6.0 1.0 -0.0 to 2.0 .060
5 8.2 8.0 0.2 -2.3 to 2.5 .941

Result.

  • Jumps matter. Adding them roughly halves the prediction error (5.3 vs 11.3 for the smooth part alone).
  • 2 and 3 stars have the same jump (3.8 and 3.7 points, difference p = .879).
  • 4 stars is a bigger jump, about twice as large (7.0 points; larger than at 2 and at 3, both p < .0005).
  • 5 stars (8.2) is not clearly larger than 4 (p = .443). It also sits at the end of the scale, so its meaning is ambiguous.
  • Left-digit is close but not complete. One inattention setting (\(\theta\) = 0.040, 95% CI 0.030-0.055) predicts almost as well (5.4) and has the best BIC. In words: people discount about 4% of the decimal part relative to the whole star. It matches the free jumps at 2 and 5 stars. But it overstates the jump at 3 (by 1.1 points, p = .009) and understates the jump at 4 (by 1.0 points, p = .060, borderline). So 3 stars is a weaker boundary, and 4 stars a stronger one, than a pure left-digit effect predicts.

Step 3: A lasting shift in sensitivity?

Question. Besides the jump at 4, do differences stay larger from some point onward, as the region models suggested?

Why. A lasting shift would mean people become more sensitive above a threshold, which is a different claim from a one-off jump. This step adds a shift that starts at a point \(r^*\) (searched from 2.0 to 4.6 stars) and stays on above it.

  • \(r^*\) = the rating where sensitivity would change, in stars.
Show code 
show_lev(c("beta", "shift"))
Model Prediction error Δ BIC
+ separate jump at 2, 3, 4 and 5 5.3 16.2
+ separate jumps + lasting sensitivity shift 5.5 26.8

Result. No. The shift does not improve prediction (5.5 vs 5.3 without it), and its best location is \(r^*\) = 4.60 stars: the top of the range searched, not near 4. The “differences stay bigger after 4” pattern in the region models is explained by the smooth rise in sensitivity plus the one-off jump at 4.

Question. Does this model describe the curve better than the three-region step model from Test 3?

Result. The best β-δ models predict held-out participants clearly better than the 3-region step model (5.3–5.4 vs 7.0), and come close to the raw averages (5.0). Of all the improvement over a straight line that is possible (reaching the raw averages), the separate-jumps model achieves 96% and the 3-region model 79%. The top four β-δ versions are close to one another, so the data do not strongly prefer one way of modeling the jumps. All agree on the shape described in Step 5.

Step 5: What the model says

The fitted curve. The orange line is the full model; the dashed blue line is its smooth part alone. The gap between them is the jumps, which appear exactly at the magenta blocks.

Show code 
p_fit <- tibble(x = L_all$xv, full = fb$fitted,
                smooth = fb$coef[["offset"]] + fb$coef[["lambda"]] * perf(round(L_all$xv - 0.2, 1), round(L_all$xv + 0.2, 1), fb$grid$c))
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = p_fit, aes(x, smooth), color = blue, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = p_fit, aes(x, full), color = orange, linewidth = 1.2) +
  cross_points(mean_curve, 2.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 5, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Midpoint of the rating pair (stars)", y = "Average perceived difference",
       title = "Smooth part (dashed blue) plus jumps (orange) against the averages (points)") +
  theme_pod

How good each rating feels. This is the value curve \(u(r)\) the model implies. Panel A rescales it so a 1-star rating = 0 and a 5-star rating = 100. Panel B removes the smooth rise and shows only what the jumps add, on the same 0–100 scale.

  • \(u(r)\) = perceived value of rating \(r\), rescaled to run from 0 (1 star) to 100 (5 stars).
Show code 
rr <- seq(1, 5, by = 0.005)
lead_hat_v <- \(v, th) fl(v) + (1 - th) * (v - fl(v))
sm_free <- fb$coef[["lambda"]] * (u_perf(rr, fb$grid$c) - u_perf(1, fb$grid$c))
jumps_free <- fb$coef[["beta2"]] * (rr >= 2) + fb$coef[["beta3"]] * (rr >= 3) +
  fb$coef[["beta4"]] * (rr >= 4) + fb$coef[["beta5"]] * (rr >= 5 - 1e-9)
u_free <- sm_free + jumps_free
sm_ld <- fl_ld$coef[["lambda"]] * (u_perf(rr, fl_ld$grid$c) - u_perf(1, fl_ld$grid$c))
u_ld  <- fl_ld$coef[["lambda"]] * (u_perf(lead_hat_v(rr, fl_ld$grid$theta), fl_ld$grid$c) - u_perf(1, fl_ld$grid$c))
k_free <- 100 / tail(u_free, 1); k_ld <- 100 / tail(u_ld, 1)
model_cols <- c(`Smooth part + separate jumps` = orange, `Smooth part only` = blue, `Left-digit version` = ink2)
model_lty  <- c(`Smooth part + separate jumps` = "solid", `Smooth part only` = "dashed", `Left-digit version` = "dotted")
pA <- bind_rows(tibble(r = rr, u = k_free * u_free, model = "Smooth part + separate jumps"),
                tibble(r = rr, u = k_free * sm_free, model = "Smooth part only"),
                tibble(r = rr, u = k_ld * u_ld, model = "Left-digit version")) |>
  ggplot(aes(r, u, color = model, linetype = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2:5, color = grid_c, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = model_lty, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Perceived value (1 star = 0, 5 stars = 100)",
       title = "A. How good each rating feels") +
  theme_pod
pB <- bind_rows(tibble(r = rr, u = k_free * jumps_free, model = "Smooth part + separate jumps"),
                tibble(r = rr, u = k_ld * (u_ld - sm_ld), model = "Left-digit version")) |>
  ggplot(aes(r, u, color = model, linetype = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2:5, color = grid_c, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = ink2, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = model_lty, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5) +
  labs(x = "Star rating", y = "Value added by the jumps\n(same 0-100 scale)",
       title = "B. What the jumps add once the smooth rise is removed") +
  theme_pod + theme(legend.position = "none")
pA / pB

Reading the panels. In panel A, the curve bends upward: each extra 0.1 star is worth more the higher the rating. In panel B, the separate-jumps model is a staircase: value steps up at each whole star, with equal steps at 2 and 3 and larger steps at 4 and 5 (the step at 5 also reflects the end of the scale). The left-digit version is a sawtooth: value lags behind within each whole star, because part of the decimal is ignored, and catches up at the next whole star. Both produce the same visible result: pairs that cross a whole star feel bigger.

Result.

  • Sensitivity roughly doubles from the bottom to the top of the scale. A 0.4-star difference near the top (4.6 vs 5.0) is worth about 2.1 times as much as the same difference near the bottom (1.0 vs 1.4), from the smooth part alone (95% CI 1.7-2.6). The anchor is \(T\) = 8.1 stars (95% CI 7.1-9.8).
  • On top of that, value jumps at every whole star. A pair that crosses 2 or 3 stars feels about 4 slider points bigger because of the jump, and one that crosses 4 stars about 7 points bigger.
  • The jumps are small next to the smooth rise. Together they add about 4 of the 100 points between a 1-star and a 5-star rating (panel B). But each one lands on just the four pairs that cross it, which is why those pairs stand out so clearly.

The breaks and slopes found on the average curve of all 187 condition 1 participants, including the 20 who failed the attention-check rule.

Result. Both kinds of model give nearly the same answers without the top pair and with all 187 participants. The 4-star jump stays about twice the jumps at 2 and 3 in every version.

Does it depend on how people use the slider?

Question. People use the slider very differently: some spread their answers widely, others barely move it. Wide-range users produce bigger swings, so they pull the average curve more. Are the Test 6 results driven by them?

Why this check. A full model of each person’s slider use is possible but complex. This simpler check splits participants into two equal halves by the spread of their own answers (the standard deviation of their 37 responses) and fits the Test 6 model separately in each half.

Raw jump sizes are bound to be bigger for wide-range users, so the groups are compared on two measures that do not depend on how widely someone uses the slider:

  • Sensitivity ratio: how much more a 0.4-star difference is worth at the top of the scale (4.6 vs 5.0) than at the bottom (1.0 vs 1.4). 1 = no change across the scale.
  • 4-star ratio: the jump at 4 stars divided by the average of the jumps at 2 and 3. 1 = 4 stars is no bigger a boundary than 2 or 3.
Show code 
grp_rows <- bind_rows(lapply(names(grp_sum), function(g) {
  s <- grp_sum[[g]]; ids <- grp_ids[[g]]; sd_g <- person_sd[ids]; Yg <- Ymat[, ids]
  tibble(Group = g, n = length(ids),
         `Response spread (SD)` = sprintf("%.0f-%.0f", min(sd_g), max(sd_g)),
         `Rise, bottom to top pair` = sprintf("%.0f", mean(Yg[nrow(Yg), ]) - mean(Yg[1, ])),
         `Sensitivity ratio` = sprintf("%.1f (%s)", s$sens, ci(s$sens_draws)),
         `Jumps at 2 / 3 / 4 / 5` = paste(sprintf("%.1f", s$fit$coef[c("beta2", "beta3", "beta4", "beta5")]), collapse = " / "),
         `4-star ratio` = sprintf("%.1f (%s)", s$j4, ci(s$j4_draws)),
         `4-star jump minus avg. of 2 and 3` = sprintf("%.1f, p %s",
                                                      s$fit$coef[["beta4"]] - (s$fit$coef[["beta2"]] + s$fit$coef[["beta3"]]) / 2,
                                                      pb_eq(s$j4_minus)))
}))
grp_rows |> kable(align = "lrrrrrrr", caption = "Test 6 model fitted separately in each half (95% bootstrap intervals in brackets)")

  geom_line(aes(x, full), color = orange, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(aes(x, m, fill = pt_type, shape = pt_type), color = "#fcfcfb", stroke = 0.4, size = 2) +

  scale_shape_manual(values = setNames(c(23, 21), cross_levels), name = NULL) +

Result.

  • Rising sensitivity does not depend on slider use. Sensitivity is about twice as high at the top as at the bottom in both groups (2.1 and 2.2), even though wide-range users’ answers rise 65 points from bottom to top and narrow-range users’ only 28 points.
  • Jumps at whole stars appear in both groups.
  • The extra-large 4-star jump is clear only among wide-range users. Their 4-star jump is 2.1 times the average of the 2- and 3-star jumps (p < .0005 for a difference). For narrow-range users it is 1.5 times, with an interval that includes 1 (p = .077). The difference between the groups is itself uncertain (p = .247). Narrow-range users’ smaller answers carry less signal relative to noise, so this may mean the effect is harder to detect in them rather than absent. Either way, the special status of 4 stars rests more heavily on wide-range users than the other findings do.

Ratios within each person

Question. If every person’s answers are put on their own scale, so wide- and narrow-range users count equally, do the Test 6 results still hold?

Why this check. Each answer is divided by that person’s own average across the 37 pairs. A value of 1.3 then means “this pair felt 30% more different than this person’s typical pair”, whatever part of the slider they used. The average is used as the reference rather than one answer (such as the first pair) because a single answer is noisy and often near 0: 12 people answered 0 for 1.0 vs 1.4, which would make their ratios impossible. Only 1 person has an average below 5. Ratios can still be extreme for a few people, so the main version combines people by the median at each pair; the mean is shown for comparison.

Show code

  `Sensitivity ratio` = sprintf("%.1f (%s)", s$sens, ci(s$sens_draws)),
  `4-star ratio` = sprintf("%.1f (%s)", s$j4, ci(s$j4_draws)),
  `4-star jump minus avg. of 2 and 3` = paste0("p ", pb_eq(s$j4_minus)))
bind_rows(rel_row(raw_sum, "Raw answers, mean (main analysis)"),
          rel_row(rel_sum[[1]], "Ratios to own average, median"),
          rel_row(rel_sum[[2]], "Ratios to own average, mean")) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr", caption = "Slider-free measures under each version (95% bootstrap intervals in brackets)")

Result.

  • Rising sensitivity holds on the ratio scale: about 2.1 times more sensitive at the top than at the bottom (median version), against 2.1 in the main analysis.
  • The jumps at whole stars hold. A pair that crosses 2 or 3 stars feels about 10% more different than a person’s typical pair because of the jump; one that crosses 4 stars about 17%.
  • The 4-star jump relative to 2 and 3: 1.6 times (median version, p = .004) and 1.9 times (mean version, p < .0005), against 1.9 in the main analysis. With every person counting equally, 4 stars is still clearly a stronger boundary than 2 or 3. The effect is slightly smaller in the median version, consistent with wide-range users showing it more strongly. This also suggests the uncertain result for narrow-range users in the previous check mostly reflects a smaller group with weaker signal, not an absent effect.

Part 4: Caveats

  • The average curve blends people. If participants put their boundaries in slightly different places, averaging smears each person’s sharp step into a gentler slope. The breaks describe the average curve, not necessarily any one person. Individual boundaries were too noisy to estimate one person at a time (pod1_analysis.qmd).
  • Regions are not labels. The models find where the curve changes. Calling regions negative, neutral or positive is an interpretation.
  • Straight lines cannot represent the whole-star bumps. Region slopes average over them, so a slope that differs from 0 does not by itself mean perception changes smoothly within the region.
  • Responses are not independent. The bootstrap and prediction test resample whole participants, which respects that each person gave 37 related answers.
  • The β-δ model is a borrowed structure, not a claim about discounting. It is used because it cleanly separates a smooth change in sensitivity from one-off jumps. “Distance from perfect” is one convenient smooth shape; others that rise toward the top might fit similarly.
  • The jump at 5 stars and the end of the scale cannot be separated. Only one pair (4.6 vs 5.0) crosses 5, and it is also the last pair on the scale.
  • The model describes the average person. Individuals may differ in how strongly they react to whole stars, and the average jump can hide that.

B. Slope checks

Two further checks of the region slopes:

  • Mixed model: all individual responses at the chosen breaks, with each participant allowed their own intercept and region slopes. Its p-values treat the breaks as known in advance, so they are somewhat too optimistic.
  • Split-half: breaks are found in a random half of participants (A), and the slopes are tested only in the other half (B), whose data played no part in placing them.

D. Whole-star bumps on a straight-line trend (earlier version of Test 6)

An earlier version of the whole-star analysis, kept for transparency. It assumed sensitivity rises in a straight line across the scale. Test 6 shows that a curved rise fits much better, and under the curved rise the jumps at 2 and 3 stars are equal. The small 3-star bump below is therefore mostly an artifact of the straight-line assumption.

This model fits one model to all individual responses with three parts: an overall upward trend, a separate bump for each whole star crossed, and a term for the top pair. The top pair crosses 5 and sits at the end of the scale, so those two cannot be separated. Each person has their own baseline and overall slope.

Show code 
tibble(Term = c("Overall trend (points per star)", "Crossing 2 stars", "Crossing 3 stars",
                "Crossing 4 stars", "Top pair (crosses 5; end of scale)"),
       key = c("x", "cross2", "cross3", "cross4", "top")) |>
  mutate(Estimate = sprintf("%.1f", ws_co[key, "Estimate"]),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", ws_co[key, "Estimate"] - 1.96 * ws_co[key, "Std. Error"],
                            ws_co[key, "Estimate"] + 1.96 * ws_co[key, "Std. Error"]),
         p = fmt_p(ws_co[key, "Pr(>|t|)"])) |>
  select(-key) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr", caption = "Extra points on the 0-100 slider")

Show code 
ws_pred <- long_ws |> distinct(x, cross2, cross3, cross4, top) |> arrange(x)
fe <- lme4::fixef(ws_each)
ws_pred$yhat <- fe["(Intercept)"] + fe["x"] * ws_pred$x + fe["cross2"] * ws_pred$cross2 +
  fe["cross3"] * ws_pred$cross3 + fe["cross4"] * ws_pred$cross4 + fe["top"] * ws_pred$top
ggplot() +
  geom_step(data = ws_pred, aes(x, yhat), color = orange, linewidth = 1.1, direction = "mid") +
  cross_points(mean_curve, 2.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 5, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Midpoint of the rating pair (stars)", y = "Average perceived difference",
       title = "Trend plus whole-star bumps (orange line) against the averages (points)") +
  theme_pod

Result.

  • Crossing a whole star matters. Adding the bumps clearly improves the fit: χ²(2) = 257.6, p < .001.
  • The whole stars are not equally strong boundaries. Letting each have its own bump fits better than forcing one shared size: χ²(2) = 47.5, p < .001. Under this straight-line version, crossing into 4 is the strongest and crossing into 3 the weakest; Test 6 revises the second part.
